source_text: CAPUT DECIMUM. Resurrectionem carnis certo futuram demonstratur e Veteri Testamento. Hactenus vidimus resurrectionem carnis esse possibilem: nunc demonstrabimus e scripturis & orthodoxa antiquitate, eam certo futuram.
english: CHAPTER TEN. The resurrection of the flesh is demonstrated to be certainly future from the Old Testament.
So far we have seen that the resurrection of the flesh is possible: now we shall demonstrate from the Scriptures and from orthodox antiquity that it is certainly future.

source_text: VII. Luculenta & viva specimina, quibus sub V.T. resurrectio mortuorum adstruitur, sunt miranda Dei opera, quibus nonnulli e morte in vitam sunt revocati. Huc pertinent filius viduae Sareptanae ab Elia, filius Sunamitidis ab Elisaeo, & vir contactis Elisaei ossibus reviviscens, 1 Reg. 17.22; 2 Reg. 4.35 & 13.21. Mirari subit quod Sadducaei tam obstinate negaverint. Occasio errandi a Sadoco e verbis Antigoni Sochaei: ne sitis tanquam servi qui ideo Domino serviunt ut demensum accipiant; jubebat non tam spe mercedis quam ex amore. Quam sententiam in deteriorem partem rapientes inferebant nullam esse benefactorum mercedem, nullam spem alterius vitae: quorsum allusit Paulus Act. 23.v.6.
english: VII. The splendid and living specimens by which under the OT the resurrection of the dead is established are God's wondrous works recalling some from death to life: the widow of Sarepta's son by Elijah, the Shunammite's son by Elisha, and the man who revived at Elisha's bones — 1 Kings 17:22; 2 Kings 4:35 and 13:21.

One wonders that the Sadducees so obstinately denied it. The occasion of erring was taken by Sadoc from Antigonus of Socho's words: Be not like servants who serve the Lord to receive a portion; he commanded not so much by hope of reward as from love. Twisting that sentence worse, they inferred no reward of good deeds, no hope of another life — to which Paul alluded in Acts 23:6.

source_text: 3. Huc pertinet illud Esa. 26.v.19. reviviscent mortui tui &c. Hunc locum de resurrectione carnis intelligunt Cyrillus Alexandrinus & Hieronymus, & his antiquiores Irenaeus lib. 5.cap.14. & Tertullianus cap. 31. Contextus Hebraeus ostendit prophetam loqui de restitutione populo Judaico post calamitates; haec tamen promissio resuscitatione mortuorum adumbratur. 4. Huc pertinet visio Ezech. 37. ossa arida &c. ubi Tertullianus de resurrectione cap. 30. Non posset de ossibus figura componi, si non idipsum ossibus eventurum esset. Theodoretus: haec non solum revocationis Judaeorum, sed etiam resurrectionis omnium hominum figura. Omitimus Hoseae 6.2. ad resurrectionem Christi; & Hoseae 13.14. quod Apostolus refert 1 Cor. 15.54.
english: (3) Isa. 26:19, Your dead shall live, &c. Cyril of Alexandria and Jerome understand this of the resurrection of the flesh, and older than these Irenaeus 5.14 and Tertullian ch. 31. The Hebrew context shows the prophet speaking of restoration for the Jewish people after calamities; yet this promise is foreshadowed by the raising of the dead.

(4) Ezek. 37, the dry bones: Tertullian On the Resurrection ch. 30 — A figure could not be composed of bones if that very thing were not going to happen to bones. Theodoret: a figure not only of recalling the Jews but of the resurrection of all men. We omit Hosea 6:2 (alluding to Christ's resurrection) and Hosea 13:14 (which the Apostle refers to the resurrection at 1 Cor. 15:54).

source_text: V. Evidens dictio V.T. de resurrectione carnis nobis exhibet partim perspicua documenta, partim luculenta & viva specimina. VI. Perspicua documenta sunt testimonia, quae nemo sanus negare potest. Huc pertinet 1. illud Dan. 12.v.2. multi ex iis qui dormiunt &c. Hac propter Johannes Chrysostomus hom. 1. de Lazaro nimis hallucinatus est, qui veteris testamenti hominibus arcanum resurrectionis dogma incognitum fuisse opinatur. 2. Huc pertinet illud Jobi 19.v.25. Equidem novi redemptorem meum vivere, & postremo super pulverem constituturum, & de carne mea videbo Deum. Recte Hieronymus epist. 61. Quid hac prophetia manifestius? Nullus tam aperte post Christum, quam iste ante Christum de resurrectione loquitur.
english: V. The evident diction of the Old Testament concerning the resurrection of the flesh exhibits partly clear documents, partly splendid and living specimens.

VI. Clear documents are testimonies which no sane person can deny. Here belongs (1) Dan. 12:2, Many of those who sleep, &c. For this reason Chrysostom in Homily 1 on Lazarus was too much hallucinating when he thought the secret dogma of the resurrection unknown to OT men. (2) Job 19:25: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he shall at last stand upon the dust, and from my flesh I shall see God. Rightly Jerome, Epistle 61: What is clearer than this prophecy? No one speaks so openly after Christ as this one before Christ concerning the resurrection.

source_text: Quaeritur, An & quomodo haec verba resurrectionem probent. Quorum Deus est Deus, illi vivunt. Atqui Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi Deus est Deus. Ergo Abraham, Isaac & Jacob vivunt. Major: vera & realis relatio est inter Deum & ipsos; si vera relatio, verum fundamentum utrinque oportet. Non igitur prorsus nihil esse possunt, sed vere aliquo modo existunt. Vivunt certe secundum animam, si non secundum corpus. Perinde fuerit si resurrectionem adversus Sadducaeos probaturus animae immortalitatem probet, quia hanc probando illam probat indirecte. Secundo sensus: non penitus divinae potentiae subtracti sunt, sed ita ei subjacent ut pro ipsius beneplacito in vitam revocari possint; hoc Lucas v.38 innuit. Quaeritur, Cur Christus per consequentiam probare voluerit, cum in V.T. perspicua testimonia occurrant? Origenes & Hieronymus annotant Sadducaeos solum Mosen recepisse. Rectius: cum Sadducaei e Mose resurrectionem impugnarent, Christus voluit eam ex eodem confirmare, adversariorum arrogantiam retundere.
english: It is asked whether and how these words prove the resurrection. Those whose God is God, they live. But God is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Therefore Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live. The major: there is a true and real relation between God and them; if a true relation, there must be a true foundation on both sides. Therefore they cannot be utterly nothing, but truly exist in some way — certainly according to the soul if not according to the body. It would be the same if, proving the resurrection against the Sadducees, he proves the soul's immortality, because by proving this he proves that indirectly.
Secondly the sense is: they are not wholly withdrawn from the divine power, but so subject to it that they can be recalled to life at his good pleasure; Luke 20:38 hints this.

Why did Christ wish to prove by consequence when clear OT testimonies occur? Origen and Jerome note that the Sadducees received Moses alone. More rightly: since the Sadducees attacked the resurrection from Moses, Christ wished to confirm it from the same and to beat back their arrogance.

source_text: Qui propius Sadducaeorum & Sadducaei Christianorum sunt, ut Tertullianus vocat negatores resurrectionis tum de carne Christi cap. 1. tum de resurrectione cap. 36. iis non immerito respondemus cum Christo, Matth. 22.v.29. Erratis, nescientes scripturas, quibus nempe Deus resurrectionem praedixit & promisit: neque potentiam Dei, per quam fiunt, quae alioquin nulla naturae potentia fieri possent, & a qua pendet resurrectio carnis. II. Est autem id demonstrandum tum e V. tum e N. Testamento.
english: Those who are nearer to the Sadducees, and the Christian Sadducees — as Tertullian calls the deniers of the resurrection, both On the Flesh of Christ ch. 1 and On the Resurrection ch. 36 — we answer not undeservedly with Christ, Matt. 22:29: You err, not knowing the Scriptures, by which God has foretold and promised the resurrection; nor the power of God, by which things are done that otherwise could be done by no power of nature, and on which the resurrection of the flesh depends.
II. And this is to be demonstrated both from the Old and from the New Testament.

source_text: III. E V.T. demonstratur vel obscurius, per justam interpretationem, vel clarius, per evidentem dictionem. IV. Obscurius per justam interpretationem demonstratur, quando firma consequentia e dicto V.T. deducitur. Luc. 20.v.27. Sadducaei opinionem suam contra Christum defendere & resurrectionem a Christo assertam destruere conabantur argumento ducente ad absurdum: Si est resurrectio mortuorum, orietur magna confusio matrimoniorum, ita ut unius mulieris septem futuri sint mariti. Atqui absurdum est consequens & contra jus naturae. Ergo & antecedens. Consequentiam probant e lege Mosis Deut. 25.v.5. Christus vero respondet, 1. negando illam consequentiam, addita ratione, quia in resurrectione nuptiae cessant, id quod plenius expressit Lucas cap. 20.v.34. 2. Novum argumentum opponendo, qua suam sententiam confirmat, De resurrectione, inquiens, non legistis, quod vobis dictum est a Deo dicente: Ego sum Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci, & Deus Jacobi?
english: III. From the Old Testament it is demonstrated either more obscurely, by just interpretation, or more clearly, by evident diction.

IV. More obscurely by just interpretation it is demonstrated when a firm consequence is drawn from a saying of the Old Testament. Luke 20:27: the Sadducees tried to defend their opinion against Christ and to overthrow the resurrection he asserted with an argument to absurdity: If there is a resurrection of the dead, a great confusion of marriages will arise, so that seven will be husbands of one woman. But the consequent is absurd and against the law of nature. Therefore so is the antecedent. They prove the consequence from Moses' law, Deut. 25:5. But Christ answers (1) by denying that consequence, because in the resurrection marriages cease (Luke 20:34 more fully); (2) by opposing a new argument: Concerning the resurrection, Have you not read what was said to you by God: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?
